# The Scope and Purpose of `composer.lock`

The statement that a `composer.lock` file "only has an effect on the main project" is often misunderstood as a limitation of the lock file itself, rather than a description of how Composer resolves dependencies across multiple repositories. To understand why this phrasing exists, we must look at how dependency resolution works in a multi-project environment versus a single-monorepo or standalone application.

When you run `composer update` in your main project (let's call it Project P), Composer downloads the lock file and validates that your `composer.json` requirements are satisfied by the versions pinned in that file. If Project P requires library A, and library A declares a dependency on library B version 1.3, Composer does not treat library B as an independent variable once the lock file is present.

In a standalone project like Project P, the lock file creates a rigid contract for the entire dependency tree. Even if library B has a new patch release (v1.4) available that fixes a bug or adds a feature, Composer will ignore it during installation unless you explicitly tell it to update the dependencies. The lock file forces the system to revert to v1.3 because that is the specific state required for Project P to function correctly with library A's current code.

This behavior addresses the core problem of non-deterministic builds. Without a lock file, every time you run `composer install` or clone your repository on a colleague's machine or a CI server, Composer might resolve library B to v1.4 because it is semantically compatible with library A. This leads to "works on my machine" scenarios where environment differences cause subtle bugs. The lock file ensures that the exact same binary files are downloaded every time, regardless of what new versions exist in Packagist or other repositories.

The confusion often arises when considering the perspective of library B's maintainers versus your project. If you publish Project P as a package on Packagist and require it to be installed by another application (let's call it Project Q), Project Q will fetch your `composer.json` and `composer.lock`. However, strictly speaking, the lock file in your repository is specific to your environment's resolution state at that moment.

If Project Q installs your package, they will receive the constraints defined in your `composer.json`, but the actual versions installed will be determined by Project Q's own `composer.lock` if you publish it with one, or by their local resolution if you don't. If you commit a specific `composer.lock` to your source code repository, you are telling anyone cloning that repo: "Do not resolve dependencies; use exactly these versions."

Consider a scenario where library A updates its `composer.json` to require library B version 1.4 but forgets to update the `composer.lock` in your repo. When Project Q installs your package, Composer will see the requirement for v1.4 and install it, effectively ignoring the old lock file content if it is out of sync or if you are using `composer install --no-dev` without a lock file present. However, if you commit both files, the lock file acts as an override that locks the entire tree to the versions tested and verified in your CI pipeline.

The point of the lock file is not to restrict the main project's ability to use newer compatible libraries, but rather to freeze the specific set of binaries that have been validated against your codebase. If library B v1.4 introduces a breaking change that breaks library A v2.0, and your `composer.lock` says you need B v1.3, Composer will refuse to install B v1.4 even though it satisfies the version constraints in `composer.json`. This protection is why automated tests are run after updating dependencies; without them, the lock file becomes a barrier that could hide incompatibilities introduced by upstream updates.

For teams using Laravel or similar frameworks where dependency stability is critical, this mechanism prevents unexpected errors when deploying to production environments that differ from local development machines. If you are maintaining a package that others depend on, you must decide whether to commit your `composer.lock` (which freezes your specific build) or to omit it (allowing consumers to resolve their own versions based on your `composer.json`). The documentation note simply clarifies that the lock file is not a global registry constraint that forces other projects to install v1.3 of library B, but rather a local directive for Project P.
